problem: Prior socially compliant navigation methods need precise positions and velocities of nearby pedestrians. These come from expensive sensors such as 3D LiDAR plus time-consuming tracking and state estimation. Pure behavior cloning from raw sensor input ignores the temporal correlation between frames, suffers compounding covariate-shift error, and generalizes poorly. IRL-based approaches are too expensive because they run RL in an inner loop.
motivation: Cheap depth cameras are well suited to mobile robots that will share spaces with people. Simulated depth images transfer to the real world much better than simulated RGB. GAIL lets a policy learn from whole expert trajectories without first recovering a reward, which could fix BC's frame-wise, reactive behaviour. It had only been shown in simulation (GAIL, InfoGAIL), not on a real robot.
key_idea: Pre-train a depth-image policy with behavior cloning on social-force-model demonstrations, then refine it with a Wasserstein-GAIL/TRPO procedure that samples trajectories asynchronously across several social scenarios, so the policy imitates trajectory-level socially compliant behaviour from raw depth.
insight: GAIL's trajectory-level (MDP-aware) imitation turns the reactive, frame-wise BC policy into a safer and usually faster one. The only comparison is BC vs. BC+GAIL (Fig. 7): GAIL gives a larger average minimum distance to pedestrians in all six scenarios. It gives shorter travel time in most scenarios, but is slightly slower in two easy ones. Qualitatively, GAIL handles the group scenarios: it passes between a group (d) and travels out of a group (e), where BC fails. Other design aids are not separately ablated: an auxiliary social-force prediction head, training across interleaved scenarios, and an added collision cost.
method: Social-force expert and simulator: a released Gazebo plugin simulates pedestrians under Helbing's social force model (desired + social force; obstacle and fluctuation forces omitted). A depth sensor mounted on a pedestrian records depth frames labeled with the social force, the desired force (normalized direction to goal) and velocity. The dataset has 10,000 state-action pairs from 6 scenarios with randomized initial configurations; 2,000 are held out.

Generator/policy network: 400×250 depth image through three streams, then concat → conv → Dense 256 → Dense 128. The streams are a pre-trained ResNet-50, a 3-layer conv stack (7×7/4, 5×5/4, 3×3/2) and a 20×20 stride-30 conv skip stream. The features are merged with the 2-D desired force, and the network outputs a 2-D action (velocity command) plus an auxiliary 2-D social-force prediction (multi-task).
Behavior cloning pre-training: supervised regression of action and social force with RMSprop (lr 1e-4, decayed ×0.9 every 20 epochs) for ~200 epochs. The result initializes the GAIL generator θ0.

Discriminator (WGAN critic): one conv stream (32/64/128 channels, 3×3, stride 4), merged with the desired force and the action, then Dense 256 → 128 → scalar score. It is trained with RMSprop lr 5e-5 and weight clipping to (−0.01, 0.01) under the Wasserstein objective.

Asynchronous GAIL: each iteration samples trajectories from randomly chosen social scenarios (3 trajectories from 6 scenarios, ~1,000 samples) and updates the critic. The generator is then updated with TRPO, using the critic score as cost plus an augmented collision penalty (following InfoGAIL). Training ran 300 iterations, ~10 h on a Tesla P100.

Deployment: the policy runs on a Turtlebot waffle with an Intel RealSense R200 (depth cropped to 400×250) and a Jetson TX2 at 15 Hz. The desired force comes from laser-based localization and random goals.

setting.backbone: CNN policy with pre-trained ResNet-50 stream + small conv streams (trained via BC then WGAN-GAIL with TRPO); CNN discriminator
setting.training_data: 10,000 simulated state-action pairs (depth + desired force → social-force-model velocity) from 6 Gazebo pedestrian scenarios (2,000 held out) for BC; then on-policy GAIL rollouts in the same 6 simulated scenarios (300 iterations, ~1,000 samples each)
setting.observation: egocentric depth image (400×250) + 2-D desired force (normalized goal direction)
setting.simulator: Gazebo (custom social-force pedestrian plugin, simulated Turtlebot3 waffle)
setting.privileged: goal direction from robot localization (GT pose in sim, laser localization in real world); no pedestrian positions/velocities used

numbers_note: Quantitative results are given only as box plots in Fig. 7: average min-dist ratio and average travel-time ratio over 10 episodes per scenario, normalized by the BC mean, for 6 custom Gazebo social scenarios. No numeric values are printed in text or tables. Real-world results are qualitative only (video).
results: In 6 simulated social scenarios (passing, overtaking, crossing; plus hard group passing/crossing), 10 test episodes each, the GAIL-refined policy has a larger average minimum distance to pedestrians than the behavior-cloning baseline in all six scenarios. It achieves shorter travel time in most scenarios but is slightly slower in two easy ones. Qualitatively, it passes between and out of pedestrian groups where BC fails. The policy runs in real time (15 Hz on a Jetson TX2) on a real Turtlebot waffle in an office, using only raw depth plus goal direction.
limitations: The small depth-camera FOV (3.5 m range) means pedestrians are perceived late, causing sudden turns; real-world performance is also limited by the Turtlebot's maximum speed.

The expert is the social force model itself (obstacle and fluctuation forces omitted), not real human demonstrations. Evaluation covers only 6 hand-designed scenarios with 10 episodes each, and the only baseline is BC.

No success or collision rates and no absolute numbers are reported (only BC-normalized ratios in plots). Real-world evaluation is qualitative, and the auxiliary social-force head and asynchronous training are not ablated.
